For example, an API plugin may be written to integrate Meerschaum's web API functionality with an existing login system, such as Google SSO. Rather than writing an API backend from the ground up, Meerschaum API plugins allow you to directly connect web requests with your custom Meerschaum back-end.

??? example "API plugin example"

    ```python
    # ~/.config/meerschaum/plugins/foo.py
    from meerschaum.plugins import api_plugin

    @api_plugin
    def init_api(app):
        @app.get('/my/new/path')
        def my_new_path():
            return {'message': 'Eureka!'}
    ```


---

# 🖥️ Web Pages and Routes

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/web-pages/

# 🖥️ Web Pages, Callbacks and Routes

Plugins add pages to the [Web Console](/reference/api-instance/web-console/) with `#!python @web_page`, make them interactive with Dash callbacks, and add API routes with `#!python @api_plugin`. This page covers who may use them (signed-in visitors or anyone), the helpers for routes (`session_user`, `mount_static`) and how to style a page (`theme`, `head`, `add_head`). The decorators themselves are introduced in [Writing Your Own Plugins](/reference/plugins/writing-plugins/#the-dash_plugin-and-web_page-decorators).

## Who may run a callback

**A console callback runs only for a visitor who is signed in.** The web console checks every callback request (`POST /dash/_dash-update-component`) for a console session, the `mrsm-session-id` cookie the login page sets. A request without one is answered with `401`, and the browser goes to the login page and comes back to the page afterwards.

That is the right default for almost every page: your callbacks read pipes, users or jobs, and anonymous visitors should not run them. A page anyone may use needs two things:

1. `#!python @web_page(..., login_required=False)`, so visitors who are not signed in see the page instead of the login form;
2. **public callbacks**, so they run for those visitors too.

Mark callbacks public in one of two ways.

=== "@web_callback(..., public=True)"

    ```python
    from meerschaum.plugins import web_page, web_callback

    @web_page('visits', login_required=False)
    def visits_page():
        from dash import html
        return html.Div([
            html.Button('Visit', id='visit-button'),
            html.Div(id='visits-out'),
        ])

    @web_callback(output='visits-out.children', inputs='visit-button.n_clicks', public=True)
    def count_visits(n_clicks):
        return f"{n_clicks or 0} visits"
    ```

    `#!python @web_callback(...)` registers a callback at the top level of your plugin, without a `@dash_plugin` function, with or without `public=True`. Name its `output`, `inputs` and `state` as `'component-id.property'` strings (one or a list), so your plugin need not import Dash, which every `mrsm` command, job and worker would then load. It also takes what `#!python @dash_app.callback(...)` takes: `Output(...)`, `Input(...)` and `State(...)` objects, `prevent_initial_call`, `running`, ...

=== "@dash_plugin(public=True)"

    ```python
    from meerschaum.plugins import dash_plugin, web_page

    @dash_plugin(public=True)
    def init_public_pages(dash_app):
        from dash import Input, Output

        @dash_app.callback(Output('greeting', 'children'), Input('name', 'value'))
        def greet(name):
            return f"Hello, {name or 'stranger'}!"
    ```

    Every callback the function registers is public (whether it uses `dash_app.callback`, `dash.callback` or `dash_extensions.enrich.callback`). Keep private callbacks in another `@dash_plugin` function.

!!! warning "Public callbacks are public"

    Anyone who can reach the console can call a public callback with any inputs. Read only what the page shows anyway, and never take a pipe's keys, a username or a query from the inputs without checking them.

??? note "What counts as a session, and the exceptions"

    - A session is the `mrsm-session-id` cookie, or the `session-store` value the console sends with a callback (`State('session-store', 'data')`), which is then copied back into the cookie.
    - A session ID is the UUID the login creates. Any other value counts as no session, so pass the value you received straight to the helpers in `meerschaum.api.dash.sessions` (`is_session_active`, `get_username_from_session`, `is_state_authenticated`) and never build one yourself.
    - The console's own login and registration callbacks and its page router are public (registration only while `api:permissions:registration:users` is on).
    - A console control that fires by itself as it renders (the Sign out button on a public page's bar) is answered with "no update" instead of `401`.
    - Signed in is not the same as allowed: a callback that changes things still checks the user, as the console's own do (`meerschaum.api.dash.sessions.is_state_authenticated`, which applies `api:permissions:actions:non_admin`).
    - Dash's own MCP server (`api:dash:mcp:enabled`) follows the same rule, and also accepts an API token (`Authorization: Bearer ...`).

!!! tip "Turning the check off"

    `mrsm start api --no-auth` needs no session for anything. To keep logins but let any callback run without a session, set this in `mrsm edit config api`:

    ```yaml
    dash:
      callbacks_require_session: false
    ```

## The signed-in user in an API route

`session_user` is a FastAPI dependency: the `User` signed in to the web console in this browser, or `401`. Routes your pages call (`fetch()`, HTMX) send the session cookie by themselves. `optional_session_user` is `None` instead of `401`.

```python
from meerschaum.plugins import api_plugin

@api_plugin
def init(app):
    import fastapi
    from meerschaum.api import session_user, optional_session_user

    @app.get('/my-plugin/me')
    def me(user=fastapi.Depends(session_user)):
        return {'username': user.username}

    @app.get('/my-plugin/greeting')
    def greeting(user=fastapi.Depends(optional_session_user)):
        return {'greeting': f"Hello, {user.username if user else 'guest'}!"}
```

For clients that are not browsers (scripts, other services), use `#!python fastapi.Depends(ScopedAuth(['pipes:read']))`, which takes API tokens and scopes (see [Security and Tokens](/reference/api-instance/tokens/)). Import from `meerschaum.api` inside your `@api_plugin` function, not at the top of the plugin: the plugin is imported by every `mrsm` command, which do not need the API's packages.

## Serving files

`mount_static(app, path, directory)` serves a directory of files (images, scripts, data exports, a built front-end) from an `@api_plugin` function:

```python
import pathlib
from meerschaum.plugins import api_plugin

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent

@api_plugin
def init(app):
    from meerschaum.api import mount_static
    mount_static(app, '/my-plugin/files', HERE / 'files')
    mount_static(app, '/my-plugin/site', HERE / 'site', auth=False, html=True)
```

- **Signed in by default.** `auth=True` needs a console session or an API token (`Authorization: Bearer ...`). A browser without one is sent to the login page and back; other clients get `401`. `auth=False` serves anyone.
- **Only that directory.** No path outside it is ever served (`..`, encoded or not, and symlinks that point outside), nor hidden files and folders (`.env`, `.git/...`).
- Files get the content types browsers expect (`text/javascript`, `text/css`, `application/wasm`, ...) and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; with `auth=True`, `Cache-Control: private, no-cache`.
- `html=True` serves `index.html` for a folder.
- A path under `/dash`, `/static`, `/_pages`, `/_mrsm`, `/webterm`, `/docs` or `/redoc` is refused.

## Styling a page

The console is dark (the Bootswatch *Darkly* theme). Choose another theme for one page with `theme`, and add tags to its `<head>` with `head`:

```python
import dash_bootstrap_components as dbc
from meerschaum.plugins import web_page

@web_page('reports', theme='light')
def reports():
    ...

@web_page(
    'brochure',
    theme=dbc.themes.LUX,
    head=[
        {'tag': 'meta', 'name': 'description', 'content': 'Our weekly numbers'},
        {'tag': 'link', 'rel': 'stylesheet', 'href': 'https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter'},
    ],
)
def brochure():
    ...
```

- `theme` is `'dark'` (the default), `'light'` (*Flatly*) or the URL of any Bootstrap stylesheet: a Bootswatch theme from `dash_bootstrap_components.themes`, or a file you serve with `mount_static`. Exactly one theme applies while the page is open, and the console's returns on other pages.
- `dark_theme` decides the `dbc_dark` component overrides, which suit dark themes: on with `'dark'`, off with `'light'` and with a custom stylesheet unless you pass `dark_theme=True` (for a dark theme such as `dbc.themes.CYBORG`).
- `head` takes HTML strings, dictionaries (`{'tag': 'meta', ...}`; the text of a `script` or `style` under `children`) and Dash components (`html.Link(...)`, `html.Script(...)`). Stylesheets and meta tags apply while the page is open; a script runs once, the first time the page opens.
- A page that returns HTML (the page contract) gets its theme and tags in its own document.

For tags on **every** page (a font, an analytics snippet, a web app manifest), call `add_head(...)` at the top level of your plugin:

```python
from meerschaum.plugins import add_head

add_head(
    '<meta name="theme-color" content="#222222">',
    {'tag': 'link', 'rel': 'manifest', 'href': '/my-plugin/files/app.webmanifest'},
)
```

## Testing your pages

The [`meerschaum.testing`](/reference/plugins/testing/) pytest plugin renders your pages and fires their callbacks, signed in or not:

```python
def test_visits_page(render_page):
    page = render_page('/dash/visits')
    assert page.callback('visits-out.children', inputs={'visit-button.n_clicks': 2}) == {
        'visits-out': {'children': '2 visits'},
    }
```


---

# 🗃️ Caching

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/caching/

# 🗃️ Caching

Some things are slow to compute: a query over a big table, a chart, a call to someone else's API. `meerschaum.utils.cache` remembers the result for a while, shares it with every process of your deployment when Valkey is around, and forgets it when the pipes it came from sync.

```python
import meerschaum as mrsm
import polars as pl
from meerschaum.utils.cache import cache

weather = mrsm.Pipe('plugin:noaa', 'weather', instance='sql:main')

@cache(ttl=300, pipes=[weather])
def daily_means(station: str):
    df = weather.get_data(params={'station': station})
    return (
        df.group_by(pl.col('timestamp').dt.date().alias('day'))
        .agg(pl.col('temperature').mean())
        .sort('day')
    )
```

The first call computes; later calls with the same arguments return the cached result until five minutes have passed or `weather` syncs, whichever comes first.

## The decorator

`#!python @cache(ttl=300, pipes=None)` (or a bare `#!python @cache`) caches a function's results by its arguments.

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ttl` | Seconds a result is kept (default `300`; `None` keeps it until a listed pipe syncs or it is evicted). |
| `pipes` | Pipes whose syncs make a result stale: a list, or a function of the call's arguments that returns them (`pipes=lambda pipe, **kw: [pipe]`). |

The decorated function also has `cache_clear()` (forget its results), `cache_key(*args, **kwargs)` and `uncached` (the function itself). Arguments that are pipes, dates, sets or DataFrames make stable keys; other objects use their `repr()`, so use it on functions rather than methods.

## Values by key

```python
from meerschaum.utils.cache import cache

cache.set('station-names', ['north', 'south'], ttl=3600)
cache.get('station-names')            # ['north', 'south']
cache.get('missing', default=[])      # []
cache.set('report', report, pipes=[weather])   # forgotten when `weather` syncs
cache.delete('station-names')
cache.clear()                         # everything cached
```

## What can be cached

JSON values (`dict`, `list`, `str`, numbers, `bool`, `None`), `datetime`, `date`, `time`, `Decimal`, `UUID` and `bytes`, and pandas and Polars DataFrames (as Arrow IPC when `pyarrow` is installed). Nothing is pickled, so nothing in Valkey can run code when it is read. Tuples come back as lists. You get a copy, from memory and Valkey alike: changing it does not change the cache.

A function whose result cannot be stored still returns it; the cache warns once and does not keep it.

## Where values live

- **Valkey**, when the connector `api:cache:connector` (default `valkey:main`) answers: the web console, its API routes, jobs and your scripts share the values. Keys start with `mrsm:cache:`.
- **Process memory** otherwise (thread-safe; at most `cache.max_entries` values and `cache.max_bytes` bytes, least recently used out first).

The cache asks Valkey once, and again a minute after it did not answer. The web console says so once at startup when your plugin uses the cache and the configured connector does not answer. Choose another connector, or none, in `mrsm edit config api`:

```yaml
cache:
  connector: valkey:cache   # or null for process memory only
```

## When a listed pipe syncs

Every sync is recorded on the pipe's instance (`pipe.get_sync_status()`): jobs, `mrsm sync pipes`, Pipelines, the API and `pipe.sync()` alike. A cached value remembers the latest recorded sync of each of its `pipes`, and a newer one makes it stale. Two syncs of a pipe a few seconds apart can be recorded as one, so the second may only be noticed at the next recorded sync or when `ttl` runs out.


---

# 🧪 Testing Plugins

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/testing/

# 🧪 Testing Plugins

`meerschaum.testing` is a [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org) plugin: your tests get a throwaway Meerschaum root, a fresh SQLite instance for each test, pipes that clean up after themselves, the web API in the test process and the console's pages as a browser sees them. Nothing touches your real configuration, instances or jobs.

## Set up

Enable it in your project's `conftest.py`:

```python
pytest_plugins = ['meerschaum.testing']
```

(or run `pytest -p meerschaum.testing`). Point it at the plugins you are testing in `pytest.ini` (or the `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` table of `pyproject.toml`):

```ini
[pytest]
mrsm_plugins_dirs = plugins
```

| Option | Command line | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `mrsm_plugins_dirs` | `--mrsm-plugins-dir PATH` (repeatable) | Plugins directories to test, relative to the ini file. |
| `mrsm_venvs_dir` | `--mrsm-venvs-dir PATH` | Keep the plugins' virtual environments here between runs (default: inside the temporary root, so packages a plugin `required` are installed once per run). |
| `mrsm_env` | `--mrsm-env NAME=VALUE` (repeatable) | Variables to set after the environment is cleaned, e.g. `MRSM_NO_AUTO_INSTALL=1` when CI installs everything beforehand. |

## Fixtures

### `mrsm_root`

The test session's temporary root and plugins directory. Every inherited `MRSM_*` variable (and `TMUX`, `TMUX_PANE`) is removed for the session and restored afterwards; Meerschaum's paths, config and connectors point at the temporary root, and so do the jobs and `mrsm` commands your tests start. Jobs run locally (never as systemd units).

```python
def test_my_action(mrsm_root):
    mrsm_root.write_plugin('greeter', '''
from meerschaum.plugins import make_action

@make_action(name='greet everyone')
def greet(**kwargs):
    return True, "Hello, everyone!"
''')
    import meerschaum as mrsm
    assert mrsm.entry(['greet', 'everyone'])[0]
```

`mrsm_root.path` and `mrsm_root.plugins_dir` are the directories; `write_plugin(name, source, files=None)` adds a plugin (and reloads plugins); `env()` is the environment for a subprocess you start yourself.

### `mrsm_instance`

A temporary SQLite instance connector, `sql:test`, with a new database for each test. It is the default instance while the test runs: `mrsm.Pipe('a', 'b')` and `mrsm` commands use it.

### `mrsm_pipe`

A factory for pipes on `mrsm_instance`, registered (unless `register=False`) and deleted after the test:

```python
def test_fetch(mrsm_pipe):
    pipe = mrsm_pipe('plugin:noaa', 'weather', columns={'datetime': 'timestamp', 'id': 'station'})
    success, message = pipe.sync(begin='2026-01-01', end='2026-01-02')
    assert success, message
    assert len(pipe.get_data()) > 0
```

### `mrsm_api`

The API host (your `@api_plugin` routes, MCP tools and the web console with your pages) built in the test process for the session, on its own SQLite instance (`sql:api_test`). Needs `pip install "meerschaum[api]"` and `httpx`.

```python
def test_my_route(mrsm_api):
    assert mrsm_api.client.get('/my-plugin/me').status_code == 401
    client = mrsm_api.client_for('alice')          # signed in: console session + bearer token
    assert client.get('/my-plugin/me').json() == {'username': 'alice'}
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `mrsm_api.app`, `mrsm_api.client` | The FastAPI app and a `TestClient` without credentials. |
| `mrsm_api.user(name, password=None, admin=None)` | The user, registered first if needed (an admin when `admin`, by default when the name is `admin`). |
| `mrsm_api.session(name)` | A console session ID (the `mrsm-session-id` cookie). |
| `mrsm_api.token(name, scopes=None)` | A bearer JWT, as `/login` issues. |
| `mrsm_api.client_for(name)` | A `TestClient` with both. |

### `render_page`

`render_page(path, as_user=None, admin=None)` renders a console or plugin page as a browser with that user's session would (anonymous when `as_user` is `None`) and returns a `RenderedPage`. Needs `pip install "meerschaum[dash]"`.

```python
def test_dashboard_page(render_page):
    page = render_page('/dash/my-plugin/dashboard', as_user='alice')
    assert 'Daily means' in page.text
    assert 'station-dropdown' in page.ids
    response = page.callback('means-graph.figure', inputs={'station-dropdown.value': 'north'})
    assert response['means-graph']['figure']['data']

def test_anonymous_visitors_are_asked_to_sign_in(render_page):
    page = render_page('/dash/my-plugin/dashboard')
    assert 'login-button' in page.ids
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `page.kind` | `'dash'` (a Dash layout) or `'html'` (a page that returns HTML). |
| `page.status`, `page.layout`, `page.html`, `page.text`, `page.ids` | What the page is, and its text and component IDs for easy assertions (`'Hello' in page` works too). |
| `page.find(component_id)` | The component, as JSON. |
| `page.callback(output, inputs=None, state=None, trigger=None)` | Fire the callback that writes `output` (`'id.property'` or a component ID) with this page's session; values by `'id.property'` (the session's `session-store` and the page's location are filled in). Returns `{component_id: {property: value}}`, `None` when nothing updated, and raises `CallbackError` (with `.status`) when the console refused, e.g. `401` without a session for a callback that is not public. |


---

# 🦀 Rust Plugins

Source: https://meerschaum.io/reference/plugins/rust-plugins/

# 🦀 Rust Plugins

A Rust plugin can be one `.rs` file. Add a command, return rows of data, or create a
connector with a few functions. Meerschaum handles building and loading it.

Save your files in the plugins directory (normally `~/.config/meerschaum/plugins`;
see [custom paths](../environment.md#mrsm_plugins_dir)). You need a Rust toolchain
with `cargo` available for the first build and after edits. The first build may
download dependencies; later runs reuse the compiled plugin.

To create a starter file, run `mrsm bootstrap plugins greetings` and choose **Rust**
when the wizard asks which language to use. If you pick an action, say `sing song`,
the starter defines `#[make_action] fn sing_song(...)`, which `mrsm sing song` runs.
The wizard offers the same features as for Python plugins. Keep the default **Single file**
for a `greetings.rs` like the ones below, or choose **Package** for a Cargo crate on the
full SDK (`greetings/Cargo.toml`, see the [advanced guide](rust-plugins/advanced.md)).
Use `mrsm edit plugins greetings` to reopen it. Upload it to a repository with
`mrsm register plugins greetings -r api:your-repo`, just as you would a Python plugin.

During a port, a native plugin shadows a Python plugin with the same name. The host warns once and loads the native implementation, including its hooks. Shadowing is transitional and discouraged. Remove the Python copy after the port. If the native plugin fails to open, the host reports the error and uses the Python copy.

## Add a command

Save this as `greetings.rs`:

```rust
/// Say hello.
#[make_action]
fn greet() {
    println!("Hello from Rust!");
}
```

Run it:

```bash
mrsm greet
```

The function name becomes the command. The `///` comment becomes its help text.
To accept names from the command line, replace the function with:

```rust
#[make_action]
fn greet(action: Vec<String>) -> (bool, String) {
    (true, format!("Hello, {}!", action.join(", ")))
}
```

`mrsm greet Alice Bob` returns `Hello, Alice, Bob!`. The returned pair contains
whether the command succeeded (`true` or `false`) and a message.

## Provide data

Save this as `readings.rs`. Each `json!` object is one row:

```rust
fn fetch() -> Vec<Value> {
    vec![json!({"id": 1, "temperature": 21.5})]
}

fn register() -> Value {
    json!({"columns": {"id": "id"}})
}
```

`fetch` supplies the data. The optional `register` function supplies Pipe settings;
here, `id` identifies each row. Register a Pipe, then sync it:

```bash
mrsm register pipe -c plugin:readings -m readings -i sql:local
mrsm sync pipes -c plugin:readings -i sql:local
```

The filename supplies the plugin name: `readings.rs` becomes `plugin:readings`.
`Value` and `json!` are available without imports. Return the final expression
without a trailing semicolon, as shown above.

## Create a connector

To provide your own connector type, put its functions in a marked module:

```rust
#[make_connector]
mod readings {
    fn fetch(connector: &Connector) -> Vec<Value> {
        vec![json!({"id": 1, "source": connector.label()})]
    }
}
```

This creates `readings:<label>` connectors. For example:

```bash
mrsm register pipe -c readings:office -m readings -i sql:local
mrsm sync pipes -c readings:office -i sql:local
```

The label is `office` in this example. Use `connector.config()` to read its
configuration. You can add `register` inside the module to supply Pipe settings.
One file may contain several actions, connector modules, and helper functions.

Python sees the same types: `mrsm.get_connector('readings:office')` returns a connector
whose `fetch()`, `register()` and other module functions run in Rust, and
`mrsm.Pipe('readings:office', 'readings', instance='sql:local')` syncs from it.

## Run code around syncs

Mark functions with `#[pre_sync_hook]` or `#[post_sync_hook]` to run them before or
after every sync, like Python's sync hooks:

```rust
#[post_sync_hook]
fn report(pipe: &Pipe, success_tuple: SuccessTuple, sync_duration: f64) -> (bool, String) {
    (true, format!("{} took {sync_duration:.1}s: {}", pipe.metric_key(), success_tuple.message))
}
```

`mrsm sync pipes` prints each hook's message. A failing hook never stops the sync.

## Talk to Meerschaum

Your functions can read and write other pipes, query the database, and keep settings.
`host` and `Query` are available without imports, like `Pipe`. This `sync` rebuilds a
pipe from another one:

```rust
fn sync(pipe: &Pipe, begin: Option<Bound>, end: Option<Bound>) -> Result<SuccessTuple> {
    // Another pipe, by its keys. It is on the same instance as `pipe`.
    let readings = host::pipe("plugin:readings", "readings", None, None)?;

    // Your plugin's settings: the `plugins: readings:` section of `mrsm edit config`.
    let factor = host::plugin_config()?["factor"].as_f64().unwrap_or(1.0);

    // Its rows between `begin` and `end`, as JSON objects.
    let mut rows = readings.get_data(begin.clone(), end.clone(), None)?;
    for row in &mut rows {
        row["temperature"] = json!(row["temperature"].as_f64().unwrap_or(0.0) * factor);
    }

    // Replace this pipe's rows between `begin` and `end` with the new ones, all at once.
    pipe.replace(rows, begin, end)
}
```

Run SQL on a pipe's database with `host::read_sql`, which returns rows:

```rust
let table = readings.target();
let counts = host::read_sql(
    pipe.instance_keys(),
    &format!("SELECT station, COUNT(*) AS n FROM {table} GROUP BY station"),
)?;
```

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `host::pipe("connector", "metric", location, instance)` | Any pipe, with its registered parameters. `None` for the location or the instance (the same instance). |
| `pipe.get_data(begin, end, params)` | The rows in `[begin, end)` matching `params`, like Python's `pipe.get_data()`. |
| `pipe.get_data_with(&Query::new().order("desc").limit(1))` | The same, with `select`, `omit`, `order` and `limit`: here, the newest row. |
| `pipe.get_rowcount(begin, end, params)` | How many rows. |
| `pipe.get_sync_time()` | The newest value of the datetime column (`None` when empty). |
| `pipe.sync(rows)` | Write rows (a pipe that is not registered yet is registered first). |
| `pipe.replace(rows, begin, end)` | Replace the rows in `[begin, end)` with `rows` in one step, so nobody sees the window half rewritten. A `None` bound comes from the rows. |
| `pipe.clear(begin, end, params)` | Delete rows; `None` bounds clear everything. |
| `pipe.exists()`, `pipe.get_columns_types()`, `pipe.target()` | Whether the table exists, its columns, its name. |
| `host::read_sql("sql:main", query)` | The rows of a query on a SQL connector. |
| `host::exec_sql("sql:main", statement)` | Run a statement that returns no rows. |
| `host::plugin_config()`, `host::write_plugin_config(&json!({...}))` | Read or replace your plugin's settings, as Python's `get_plugin_config()` does. |

These work in the functions Meerschaum calls: `fetch`, `sync`, `register`, `setup`, hooks,
actions, streams, executors, routes, MCP entries and console pages. In routes, MCP entries and
pages they act for the caller, who needs the matching scope
([details](rust-plugins/advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum)). Bounds are `Bound::Int(5)`, `Bound::from("2024-01-01")` or a value
you were given; `bound.timestamp()` turns a datetime bound into Unix seconds and
`Bound::from_timestamp(seconds)` back. Each call returns a `Result`, so end it with `?`.
Writes to a protected instance are refused unless you pass `--allow-protected`.

## Add flags, a version, and setup

Give your commands their own flags with `#[add_plugin_argument(...)]`, which takes the
same arguments as Python's `add_plugin_argument` (except `nargs`; pick flags the built-in
CLI does not already use, see `mrsm --help`):

```rust
const VERSION: &str = "1.0.0";

#[add_plugin_argument("--loud", action = "store_true", help = "Shout.")]
#[make_action]
fn greet(kwargs: &Value) -> (bool, String) {
    let text = if kwargs["loud"] == true { "HELLO!" } else { "Hello!" };
    (true, text.to_string())
}

fn setup() -> (bool, String) {
    (true, "Ready.".into())
}
```

`mrsm greet --loud` returns `HELLO!`. `VERSION` is the plugin's version when you
share it through a repository, and `setup` runs during `mrsm setup plugins greetings`.
List Python packages or other plugins your plugin needs in
`const REQUIRED: &[&str] = &["plugin:other"];`, like Python's `required`.

## Serve HTTP routes and MCP tools

Mark a function with `#[api_route(...)]` to serve it from `mrsm start api`, next to the
core API, like Python's `@api_plugin`:

```rust
/// One item.
#[api_route(GET, "/greetings/items/{id}", scopes = ["pipes:read"])]
fn item(request: &RouteRequest) -> Value {
    json!({"id": request.path_param("id"), "user": request.principal})
}
```

Callers need the API's credentials and every listed scope; add `public = true` (and no
scopes) for a route anyone may call. Return JSON, text, bytes or a `RouteResponse`.
A route's [host calls](#talk-to-meerschaum) act for its caller: reading pipes needs the
`pipes:read` scope, syncing `pipes:write`, clearing `pipes:delete`, and registering
`pipes:register`. Pipe visibility, edit rights and connector teams apply too. A public route's
anonymous callers have no scopes; to serve Everyone's pipe data, add
`host_scopes = ["pipes:read"]`.

Mark functions with `#[mcp_tool]`, `#[mcp_resource]` or `#[mcp_prompt]` to offer them
to AI agents through `/mcp` and `mrsm start mcp`:

```rust
/// Add two integers.
#[mcp_tool(input_schema = r#"{"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}}}"#)]
fn add(arguments: &Value) -> Value {
    json!({"sum": arguments["a"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0) + arguments["b"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)})
}
```

The `///` comment is the tool's description.

## Run jobs and stream data

Mark a module with `#[make_executor]` to run Meerschaum jobs your own way: the jobs of
`-e procs:<label>` (for example `mrsm sync pipes -d -e procs:main`) go to its functions,
which are the executor's methods. Leave out the ones you do not need:

```rust
#[make_executor]
mod procs {
    fn get_job_names() -> Vec<String> {
        vec![]
    }
    fn create_job(name: &str, sysargs: Vec<String>) -> (bool, String) {
        (true, format!("Would run `mrsm {}` as '{name}'.", sysargs.join(" ")))
    }
}
```

Add `fn subscribe` to a connector module to stream rows into `mrsm sync pipes --listen`
as they arrive. It returns a closure the host calls for each batch:

```rust
#[make_connector]
mod ticker {
    fn subscribe() -> impl FnMut(Duration) -> Batch {
        let mut next = 0;
        move |_timeout| {
            next += 1;
            std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
            Batch::Rows(vec![json!({"id": next})])
        }
    }
}
```

## Store pipes and add console pages

Add `instance` to a connector module to make it a Meerschaum instance: `-i memory:main`
then registers, syncs and lists pipes through the functions named after the instance
methods (`register_pipe`, `sync_pipe`, `get_pipe_data`, `fetch_pipes_keys`, ...):

```rust
#[make_connector(instance)]
mod memory {
    fn register_pipe(pipe: &Pipe) -> SuccessTuple {
        SuccessTuple::ok(format!("Registered {}.", pipe.metric_key()))
    }
    fn sync_pipe(pipe: &Pipe, data: Vec<Value>) -> (bool, String) {
        (true, format!("Received {} rows.", data.len()))
    }
}
```

From Python, pass `instance='memory:main'` to `mrsm.Pipe()` or `mrsm.get_pipes()`.

Mark a function with `#[web_page]` to add a page to the web console
(`pip install meerschaum[dash]`), as Python's `@web_page` does:

```rust
#[web_page("readings/report", login_required = false)]
fn report(page: &PageRequest) -> String {
    format!("<h3>Readings</h3><p>Hello, {}.</p>", page.username.as_deref().unwrap_or("guest"))
}
```

## Every attribute

| Attribute or function | Python equivalent | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `#[make_action]` | `@make_action` | `#[make_action] fn greet(action: Vec<String>) -> (bool, String)` |
| `#[make_connector]` module | `@make_connector` | `#[make_connector] mod readings { fn fetch() -> Vec<Value> { ... } }` |
| `#[make_connector(instance)]` module | `@make_connector` with `IS_INSTANCE = True` | `#[make_connector(instance)] mod memory { fn sync_pipe(pipe: &Pipe, data: Vec<Value>) -> SuccessTuple { ... } }` |
| `fn fetch` / `fn sync` / `fn register` | `fetch` / `sync` / `register` | `fn fetch(pipe: &Pipe) -> Vec<Value>` |
| `fn subscribe` (top level or in a connector) | an `IS_STREAMING` connector's `subscribe` | `fn subscribe(pipe: &Pipe) -> impl FnMut(Duration) -> Batch` (or `Box<dyn Subscription>`) |
| `fn setup` | `setup` | `fn setup() -> bool { true }` |
| `#[pre_sync_hook]` / `#[post_sync_hook]` | `@pre_sync_hook` / `@post_sync_hook` | `#[post_sync_hook] fn report(success_tuple: SuccessTuple)` |
| `#[add_plugin_argument(...)]` | `add_plugin_argument` | `#[add_plugin_argument("--loud", action = "store_true")]` |
| `const VERSION` / `const REQUIRED` | `__version__` / `required` | `const VERSION: &str = "1.0.0";` |
| `#[api_route(...)]` | `@api_plugin` routes | `#[api_route(POST, "/my/items", scopes = ["pipes:write"])]` |
| `#[mcp_tool(...)]` | MCP tools | `#[mcp_tool(description = "Count the items.", read_only = true)] fn count() -> Value` |
| `#[mcp_resource(...)]` | MCP resources | `#[mcp_resource(uri_template = "my://items/{id}", description = "One item.")] fn item(resource: &ResourceRead) -> String` |
| `#[mcp_prompt(...)]` | MCP prompts | `#[mcp_prompt(arguments = ["who"])] fn greet(prompt: &PromptGet) -> String` |
| `#[make_executor]` module | `@make_executor` | `#[make_executor] mod procs { fn start_job(name: &str) -> (bool, String) { ... } }` |
| `#[web_page(...)]` | `@web_page` | `#[web_page("my/page", login_required = false)] fn page(page: &PageRequest) -> String` |

The [single-file reference](rust-plugins/advanced.md#single-file-reference) lists every
parameter, option and return type.

## Add dependencies

To use another Rust crate, put a Cargo dependency block at the top of your file:

```rust
//! ```cargo
//! [dependencies]
//! regex = "1"
//! ```
```

Then import it normally, for example `use regex::Regex;`. Versions and features
use standard Cargo syntax. Meerschaum builds the dependencies and keeps the
lockfile in its cache; no separate `Cargo.toml` is needed.

## Learn more

Run `mrsm show plugins` to check discovery, or `mrsm greet --help` for an action's
help. Editing a file triggers a rebuild on the next command that loads plugins.
Only run plugins you trust.

See the [single-file reference](rust-plugins/advanced.md#single-file-reference)
for optional arguments, hooks, flags, setup, routes, MCP entries, executors, streams,
[host calls](rust-plugins/advanced.md#talking-to-meerschaum), sync overrides, and dependency
details.
The [advanced guide](rust-plugins/advanced.md) covers Cargo packaging, the full SDK,
web extensions, testing, and distribution.
